issues.legal_issue: A mandatory presumption that a certified copy is genuine arises only when it is issued substantially in the legally prescribed form and manner, and any such presumption is rebuttable.
material_facts: The appellants relied on a certified copy of a land record to support their claim to tenancy.
The record did not show that the prescribed diary entry had been made or that the required fee had been noted on the extract.
The lower courts rejected the document as not genuine based on its internal features and other evidence.
issues.conclusion: The courts were not bound to presume the copy genuine because the prescribed procedure was not shown to have been substantially followed; in any event, any rebuttable presumption was displaced by the evidence.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 79 and 4 of the Evidence Act, a court presumes a qualifying certified document genuine, and presumes the certifying officer held the stated official character, only where the document substantially conforms to the legally prescribed form and manner. The presumption is rebuttable and operates until disproved.

predicates.appellate_challenge_to_documentary_presu: A party in an appeal challenged a court's treatment of a certified copy as genuine.
predicates.copy_issued_in_required_form_and_manner: The certified copy was issued substantially in the form and manner prescribed for that kind of document.
predicates.authenticity_disproved: The evidence, including the document's contents or other evidence, disproved the copy's genuineness.

issues.definition: When a documentary-presumption challenge is made, the court need not presume a certified copy genuine if the required issuance procedure was not followed or its genuineness was disproved.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory ejectment suit against a person occupying land without title falls within the jurisdiction of the revenue court.
material_facts: The landholder brought suits seeking ejectment of persons alleged to occupy his land without title.
The courts found that the disputed land was the landholder's sir land and that the appellants were not tenants.
The Board of Revenue rejected the appellants' objection that the suits were not triable by a revenue court.
issues.conclusion: The suits under section 180 were maintainable in the revenue court.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 180 and 242 of the U. P. Tenancy Act, 1939, read with the Fourth Schedule's description of a section 180 suit, place suits to eject persons occupying land without title within the revenue court's jurisdiction. The Act gives revenue courts exclusive jurisdiction over the specified disputes between landlords and tenants, while proprietary-right disputes are left to civil courts.

predicates.revenue_ejectment_suit_for_occupant_with: A claimant brought a revenue-court suit to eject a person alleged to occupy land without title.

issues.definition: A revenue-court ejectment suit against an alleged occupant without title is within the revenue court's jurisdiction.

issues.legal_issue: A provisional criminal-court order declaring possession does not give an occupant title or a right to possession that defeats an ejectment suit, and possession unlawful from its inception is not lawful retention.
material_facts: The appellants claimed that they had been admitted as hereditary tenants, but the courts found that they had not been admitted with the landholder's consent and had no tenancy rights.
A magistrate acting to prevent a breach of the peace found the appellants in possession on a specified date and ordered that they remain in possession until evicted in due course of law.
The magistrate did not direct delivery of possession to the appellants or decide title or the parties' underlying right to possession.
The appellants' possession was found to be illegal from its inception.
issues.conclusion: The magistrate's provisional order did not allow the appellants to resist the section 180 ejectment suits; their possession was not possession in accordance with law, and they could be treated as persons taking possession rather than lawfully taking and then illegally retaining it.
issues.legal_principle: Section 180 of the U. P. Tenancy Act, 1939, permits ejectment of a person taking or retaining possession without the consent of the person entitled to admit him and otherwise than in accordance with law. In that provision, taking and retaining refer to distinct situations: unlawful possession from the outset, and possession initially taken lawfully but retained illegally. Sections 145(1) and 145(6) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, authorize a magistrate to determine actual possession for the limited purpose of preventing a breach of the peace; they do not confer title or a right to possession. The provisional order decides no question of title, as explained in Dinomoni Chowdhrani v. Brojo Mohini Chowdhrani, (1901) L.R. 29 I.A. 24.

rule.if: ejectment_proceeding_against_occupant_without_title and not possession_with_landholder_consent and (possession_based_only_on_provisional_order or possession_lacked_lawful_title)

predicates.ejectment_proceeding_against_occupant_wi: A person claiming the right to admit an occupant brought an ejectment proceeding against a person alleged to have no title.
predicates.possession_with_landholder_consent: The occupant took or held possession with the consent of the person entitled to admit the occupant.
predicates.possession_based_only_on_provisional_ord: The occupant relied on a temporary order that recorded possession to prevent a breach of the peace without deciding title or authorizing delivery of possession.
predicates.possession_lacked_lawful_title: The occupant's possession was not supported by a lawful title or right to possession.

issues.definition: In an ejectment proceeding against an occupant without title, a temporary possession order does not bar ejectment where the occupant lacked the landholder's consent and relied only on that order or otherwise lacked lawful title.

issues.legal_issue: Concurrent factual findings may be accepted on appeal when they are based on the evidence and are not vitiated by an error of law.
material_facts: Three courts concurrently found, on oral and documentary evidence, that the appellants were not hereditary tenants.
The Supreme Court considered the appellants' asserted errors in the assessment of that evidence and found no basis to overturn the findings as legally erroneous.
issues.conclusion: The concurrent finding that the appellants were not hereditary tenants was accepted.
issues.legal_principle: The Court followed its usual practice of accepting a concurrent finding of fact where it is not vitiated by an error of law.

rule.if: appeal_from_concurrent_factual_findings and findings_based_on_evidence and not findings_vitiated_by_error_of_law

predicates.appeal_from_concurrent_factual_findings: A party appealed after multiple lower courts made the same factual finding.
predicates.findings_based_on_evidence: The lower courts reached the finding after considering the evidence before them.
predicates.findings_vitiated_by_error_of_law: The concurrent factual finding was affected by an error of law.

issues.definition: On an appeal from concurrent factual findings based on evidence, the findings are accepted when they are not vitiated by an error of law.

issues.legal_issue: A damages objection not pursued in the intermediate appeals and not raised in the appellant's statement of case need not be entertained at the final appellate stage.
material_facts: The trial court awarded damages despite noting that no witness had testified about damages and that the claimant's counsel had not argued the point.
The appellants did not challenge the damages award in either intermediate appeal, and their statement of case in the Supreme Court disclosed no grievance about it.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to entertain the damages objection at that stage.
issues.legal_principle: The Court did not consider it justified to permit the objection to be raised at the final appellate stage after it had not been pursued in the intermediate appeals or stated as a grievance in the case presented to the Court.

predicates.final_appeal_challenges_damages: A party raised an objection to a damages award in a final appeal.
predicates.damages_objection_not_raised_in_intermed: The party did not challenge the damages award in the intermediate appellate proceedings.
predicates.no_damages_grievance_in_appellate_case: The party's statement of case in the final appeal did not identify the damages award as a grievance.

issues.definition: A court need not entertain a damages objection raised in a final appeal when it was not pursued in intermediate appeals and was not identified as a grievance in the appellate case.

issues.legal_issue: A suit restarted under the original stay rules does not abate under amended rules when it is no longer stayed under those rules, and the amended abatement provision does not apply to excluded land where the defendant acquired no relevant rights.
material_facts: The suits were initially stayed under the original rules and were restarted under those rules before the rules were amended.
No stay was imposed under the amended rules after the suits were restarted.
The courts found the disputed land to be sir land and the appellants to be trespassers who had acquired no relevant rights under the land-reform legislation.
The Board of Revenue had previously rejected the appellants' abatement contention, and that decision had become final.
issues.conclusion: The suits could not be abated under the amended rules.
issues.legal_principle: Under rules 4 and 5 of the U. P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Rules, 1952, as amended, abatement applied to a suit stayed under the relevant rule. The amended rules differed from the original rules by excluding specified suits concerning an intermediary's sir, khudkhast, or grove land where the defendant had acquired no relevant rights, and they did not provide the original procedure for restarting a stayed suit. The Court also noted that the prior ruling on abatement had become final.

rule.if: abatement_challenge_in_stayed_suit and ((restarted_under_original_rules and not later_stayed_under_amended_rules) or (land_was_excluded_intermediary_land and defendant_acquired_no_relevant_rights) or (prior_abatement_ruling_became_final))

predicates.abatement_challenge_in_stayed_suit: A party claimed that a suit previously affected by a stay had abated under amended procedural rules.
predicates.restarted_under_original_rules: The suit was restarted under the rules in force before amendment.
predicates.later_stayed_under_amended_rules: The suit was subsequently stayed under the amended rules.
predicates.land_was_excluded_intermediary_land: The land fell within a category excluded from the amended stay provision when the defendant had not acquired the specified rights.
predicates.defendant_acquired_no_relevant_rights: The defendant had acquired none of the rights relevant to the amended exception.
predicates.prior_abatement_ruling_became_final: An earlier ruling rejecting the abatement claim became final.

issues.definition: A suit challenged as abated under amended rules is not abated where it was restarted and was not later stayed, where the land and the defendant's rights bring it within the exclusion, or where a prior ruling rejecting abatement became final.
